question: What is CSS and what is it used for?
options: A: A programming language used to create web applications.
B: A stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of a document written in HTML or XML.
C: A database query language.
D: A server-side scripting language.
correctAnswer: B: A stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of a document written in HTML or XML.
explanation: CSS is a stylesheet language that defines how HTML elements are rendered.

question: What are the different ways to add CSS to an HTML document?
options: A: Only through external stylesheets.
B: Through inline styles, internal stylesheets, and external stylesheets.
C: Only through internal stylesheets.
D: Through JavaScript only.
correctAnswer: B: Through inline styles, internal stylesheets, and external stylesheets.
explanation: CSS can be added inline, in a <style> tag, or via an external .css file.

question: What is the difference between inline, internal, and external CSS?
options: A: Inline CSS is applied directly to an element, internal CSS is defined in a <style> tag, external CSS is in a separate .css file.
B: All three are the same.
C: Inline CSS is in a separate file, internal is in <style>, external is in the element.
D: Only inline CSS is allowed.
correctAnswer: A: Inline CSS is applied directly to an element, internal CSS is defined in a <style> tag, external CSS is in a separate .css file.
explanation: Each method scopes CSS differently: inline is per element, internal is per page, external is shared.

question: What is the difference between margin and padding in CSS?
options: A: Margin is inside the border, padding is outside.
B: Margin is outside the border, padding is inside.
C: Margin and padding are the same.
D: Margin is for text, padding is for images.
correctAnswer: B: Margin is outside the border, padding is inside.
explanation: Margin creates space outside the element’s border; padding creates space inside the border.

question: What is the CSS Box Model?
options: A: It defines how elements are displayed as boxes with content, padding, border, and margin.
B: It is a model for database tables.
C: It is a way to layout tables.
D: It is a CSS framework.
correctAnswer: A: It defines how elements are displayed as boxes with content, padding, border, and margin.
explanation: The box model describes the layout of elements including content, padding, border, and margin.

question: What is the difference between border-box and content-box in box-sizing?
options: border-box includes padding and border in width/height, content-box excludes them.
border-box excludes padding and border, content-box includes them.
border-box only affects margin, content-box only affects padding.
border-box is default, content-box is not supported.
correctAnswer: border-box includes padding and border in width/height, content-box excludes them.
explanation: In border-box the specified width/height includes the element’s padding and border, while in content-box the width/height refers only to the content area.

question: What is the difference between class selectors and id selectors in CSS?
options: Class selectors target elements with a class attribute; id selectors target elements with a unique id attribute.
Class selectors are case-sensitive; id selectors are not.
Class selectors can be used only once per page; id selectors can be reused.
Class selectors are defined with #, id selectors with .
correctAnswer: Class selectors target elements with a class attribute; id selectors target elements with a unique id attribute.
explanation: Class selectors ('.class') can be applied to many elements, whereas id selectors ('#id') must be unique to a single element.

question: What are CSS selectors and what are the different types?
options: CSS selectors are patterns used to select elements; types include element, class, id, attribute, pseudo-class, pseudo-element, combinator.
CSS selectors are only element names; types include only element and class.
CSS selectors are JavaScript functions; types include function, variable, object.
CSS selectors are not used in CSS; they are used in HTML.
correctAnswer: CSS selectors are patterns used to select elements; types include element, class, id, attribute, pseudo-class, pseudo-element, combinator.
explanation: Selectors allow CSS to target elements in many ways, from simple tag names to complex combinations and pseudo-classes.

question: What is the difference between relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning in CSS?
options: Relative positions relative to its normal spot; absolute relative to nearest positioned ancestor; fixed relative to viewport; sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll.
Relative moves element to top-left; absolute moves to bottom-right; fixed moves to center; sticky moves to top.
All four are the same except sticky is deprecated.
Relative is static; absolute is static; fixed is static; sticky is static.
correctAnswer: Relative positions relative to its normal spot; absolute relative to nearest positioned ancestor; fixed relative to viewport; sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll.
explanation: Each positioning scheme defines how an element is placed: relative offsets its normal position, absolute removes it from flow relative to an ancestor, fixed ties it to the viewport, and sticky behaves like relative until a threshold is crossed.

question: What is the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden?
options: display:none removes element from layout flow; visibility:hidden keeps space but hides content.
display:none hides element but keeps space; visibility:hidden removes element from flow.
display:none and visibility:hidden are identical.
display:none shows element; visibility:hidden hides element.
correctAnswer: display:none removes element from layout flow; visibility:hidden keeps space but hides content.
explanation: display:none causes the element to be omitted from the document flow entirely, while visibility:hidden makes it invisible but still occupies its allocated space.

question: What are the different values of the display property?
options: block, inline, flex, grid
table, list-item, none, inline-block
block, inline, flex, grid, table, none, inline-block, list-item
all of the above
correctAnswer: block, inline, flex, grid, table, none, inline-block, list-item
explanation: The display property accepts many keyword values; the most common are block, inline, flex, grid, table, none, inline-block, and list-item.

question: What is the difference between em, rem, px, and % units in CSS?
options: em is relative to the parent element’s font size, rem is relative to the root font size, px is an absolute unit, % is relative to the parent element’s size
em is relative to the root font size, rem is relative to the parent element’s font size, px is relative to the parent element’s size, % is relative to the root element’s size
em is relative to the element’s font size, rem is relative to the root font size, px is an absolute unit, % is relative to the parent element’s width
all of the above
correctAnswer: em is relative to the parent element’s font size, rem is relative to the root font size, px is an absolute unit, % is relative to the parent element’s size
explanation: em scales with the element’s font-size, rem with the root’s font-size, px is fixed, and % scales relative to the parent’s dimensions.

question: What is the color property vs background-color property?
options: color sets the text color of an element, background-color sets the background color of an element
color sets the background color, background-color sets the text color
color sets the border color, background-color sets the background image
color sets the font style, background-color sets the font weight
correctAnswer: color sets the text color of an element, background-color sets the background color of an element
explanation: The color property controls the foreground (text) color, while background-color controls the element’s background.

question: What is the difference between a CSS combinator and a selector?
options: A combinator defines the relationship between two selectors, while a selector matches elements
A combinator matches elements, while a selector defines the relationship
A combinator is a property, and a selector is a value
A combinator is a pseudo-class, and a selector is a pseudo-element
correctAnswer: A combinator defines the relationship between two selectors, while a selector matches elements
explanation: Selectors identify elements; combinators (>, +, ~, space) describe how selectors relate to each other.

question: What is the purpose of the CSS reset or normalize.css?
options: To remove default browser styles for consistency across browsers
To add new styles to a page
To increase page load speed
To create animations
correctAnswer: To remove default browser styles for consistency across browsers
explanation: Reset/normalize.css neutralizes browser default styling so developers start from a consistent baseline.

question: What is Flexbox in CSS? Explain the main properties.
options: A layout model that arranges elements in a single line or column, using properties like flex-direction, justify-content, align-items.
A grid system for two-dimensional layouts using rows and columns.
A way to animate elements with keyframes.
A method to apply styles to pseudo-classes.
correctAnswer: A layout model that arranges elements in a single line or column, using properties like flex-direction, justify-content, align-items.
explanation: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout model that uses properties such as flex-direction, justify-content, and align-items to control the arrangement of items.

question: What is CSS Grid and how does it differ from Flexbox?
options: Grid is a two-dimensional layout system using rows and columns, whereas Flexbox is one-dimensional.
Grid is used only for background images.
Grid is a JavaScript library.
Grid and Flexbox are identical.
correctAnswer: Grid is a two-dimensional layout system using rows and columns, whereas Flexbox is one-dimensional.
explanation: CSS Grid handles both rows and columns simultaneously, making it a two-dimensional layout system, while Flexbox handles only one dimension at a time.

question: What is the difference between justify-content and align-items in Flexbox?
options: justify-content aligns items along the main axis, align-items along the cross axis.
justify-content aligns items along the cross axis, align-items along the main axis.
Both align items on the same axis.
justify-content only works in Grid.
correctAnswer: justify-content aligns items along the main axis, align-items along the cross axis.
explanation: justify-content distributes space along the main axis (row or column), whereas align-items distributes space along the cross axis.

question: What is the flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis property used for?
options: They control how flex items grow, shrink, and set the initial main size.
They set font size and line height.
They define border radius.
They are used for positioning elements absolutely.
correctAnswer: They control how flex items grow, shrink, and set the initial main size.
explanation: flex-grow determines how much an item grows relative to others, flex-shrink how it shrinks, and flex-basis sets its initial size before growth or shrinkage.

question: What is the difference between grid-template-columns and grid-template-areas?
options: grid-template-columns defines column sizes, grid-template-areas defines named grid areas.
grid-template-columns defines row sizes, grid-template-areas defines column sizes.
Both define the same thing.
grid-template-areas is only for CSS variables.
correctAnswer: grid-template-columns defines column sizes, grid-template-areas defines named grid areas.
explanation: grid-template-columns sets the width of each column, while grid-template-areas assigns named areas that can be referenced in grid placement.

question: What is the difference between fr unit in CSS Grid and percentage widths?
options: fr distributes remaining space after fixed-size tracks, percentages are relative to parent width.
fr is only for flexbox, percentages only for grid.
fr units are absolute pixel values, percentages are relative to viewport.
fr units cannot be used with minmax, percentages can.
correctAnswer: fr distributes remaining space after fixed-size tracks, percentages are relative to parent width.
explanation: The fr unit represents a fraction of the free space in a grid container after accounting for fixed tracks, while percentages are calculated relative to the size of the parent element.

question: What is the difference between static, relative, and floated positioning?
options: static is default, relative moves element without affecting layout, floated removes element from normal flow and allows text wrap.
static moves element relative to viewport, relative is default, floated is same as relative.
static removes element from flow, relative keeps it, floated keeps it in flow.
static is only for tables, relative for flex, floated for grid.
correctAnswer: static is default, relative moves element without affecting layout, floated removes element from normal flow and allows text wrap.
explanation: Static is the default positioning; relative offsets the element but still occupies its original space; floated elements are removed from the normal flow, allowing surrounding content to wrap around them.

question: What is a float in CSS and why is it less commonly used for layout today?
options: Float moves element left/right, used for text wrapping; less used because flexbox and grid provide better layout control.
Float centers elements horizontally; less used because it breaks mobile layouts.
Float is a CSS property for animations; less used because JavaScript does it better.
Float is a property for background images; less used due to performance issues.
correctAnswer: Float moves element left/right, used for text wrapping; less used because flexbox and grid provide better layout control.
explanation: Floats were originally designed to allow text to wrap around images; modern layout techniques like Flexbox and Grid offer more robust and predictable control, making floats less common.

question: What is the clearfix technique and why is it needed?
options: clearfix adds a pseudo-element to clear floats, preventing container collapse.
clearfix removes all floats from a page.
clearfix is a CSS reset for margins.
clearfix sets display to block for all elements.
correctAnswer: clearfix adds a pseudo-element to clear floats, preventing container collapse.
explanation: The clearfix hack inserts a pseudo-element that clears floated children, ensuring that a container expands to contain its floated descendants.

question: What is the difference between inline-block and block display?
options: block starts on new line and takes full width; inline-block flows inline but respects width/height.
block is inline-level, inline-block is block-level.
block cannot have margins, inline-block can.
block is only for images, inline-block for text.
correctAnswer: block starts on new line and takes full width; inline-block flows inline but respects width/height.
explanation: Block-level elements begin on a new line and occupy the full available width, whereas inline-block elements behave like inline elements but can have explicit width and height set.

question: How do you center an element horizontally and vertically using CSS?
options: Using margin: auto; and text-align: center;
Using flexbox with justify-content: center; align-items: center;
Using grid with grid-template-columns: 1fr; grid-template-rows: 1fr;
Using position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
correctAnswer: Using flexbox with justify-content: center; align-items: center;
explanation: Flexbox’s justify-content and align-items properties center items along the main and cross axes, respectively.

question: What is the difference between CSS Grid's implicit and explicit grid?
options: Implicit grid is defined by the author, explicit grid is auto-generated.
Explicit grid is defined by the author, implicit grid is auto-generated when content overflows.
Both are the same, just terminology.
Implicit grid only applies to flex containers.
correctAnswer: Explicit grid is defined by the author, implicit grid is auto-generated when content overflows.
explanation: Explicit grid tracks are set with grid-template-rows/columns; implicit tracks are created automatically for items that exceed those tracks.

question: What is the gap property in Flexbox and Grid?
options: It sets the spacing between grid cells only.
It sets the spacing between flex items only.
It sets the spacing between both grid cells and flex items.
It is a deprecated property.
correctAnswer: It sets the spacing between both grid cells and flex items.
explanation: The gap property works in both flex and grid layouts to define space between items or cells.

question: What is the difference between align-content and align-items in Flexbox?
options: align-items aligns individual items, align-content aligns the whole flex container's content.
align-items aligns the whole flex container, align-content aligns individual items.
Both are synonyms.
align-content only works in grid.
correctAnswer: align-items aligns individual items, align-content aligns the whole flex container's content.
explanation: align-items aligns each flex item along the cross axis; align-content aligns the collection of flex lines within the container.

question: What is subgrid in CSS Grid and what problem does it solve?
options: It allows a grid item to inherit its parent's grid tracks, solving nested grid alignment.
It creates a sub-grid for each flex item.
It is a feature for subpixel rendering.
It is a deprecated property.
correctAnswer: It allows a grid item to inherit its parent's grid tracks, solving nested grid alignment.
explanation: Subgrid lets a nested grid use the parent grid’s track definitions, keeping alignment consistent across nested grids.

question: What is the order property in Flexbox used for?
options: Determines the order of flex items along the main axis.
Sets the flex grow factor.
Specifies the flex basis.
Controls the flex shrink factor.
correctAnswer: Determines the order of flex items along the main axis.
explanation: The order property reorders flex items within a flex container without changing the source order.

question: What is z-index and how does stacking context affect it?
options: z-index controls the stacking order of positioned elements; stacking context limits z-index to its own context.
z-index sets the opacity of elements; stacking context changes background color.
z-index defines the element's width; stacking context defines height.
z-index is only for inline elements; stacking context is irrelevant.
correctAnswer: z-index controls the stacking order of positioned elements; stacking context limits z-index to its own context.
explanation: z-index only applies to positioned elements and is evaluated within the nearest stacking context, which can be created by certain CSS properties.

question: What creates a new stacking context in CSS?
options: Any element with position relative and z-index not auto.
Elements with opacity less than 1, transform, filter, perspective, etc.
Only the root element creates a stacking context.
Elements with display flex.
correctAnswer: Elements with opacity less than 1, transform, filter, perspective, etc.
explanation: These properties trigger a new stacking context, isolating z-index values from the rest of the document.

question: What are CSS pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements? Give examples.
options: Pseudo-classes target elements in a specific state like :hover; pseudo-elements target parts like ::before.
Pseudo-classes are for styling text; pseudo-elements are for layout.
Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are the same thing.
Pseudo-classes target classes; pseudo-elements target IDs.
correctAnswer: Pseudo-classes target elements in a specific state like :hover; pseudo-elements target parts like ::before.
explanation: Pseudo-classes (e.g., :hover) apply to element states, while pseudo-elements (e.g., ::before) style virtual elements.

question: What is CSS specificity and how is it calculated?
options: Specificity is a weight based on selectors; calculated by counting IDs, classes, and elements.
Specificity is the color of the text; calculated by RGB values.
Specificity is the font size; calculated by px values.
Specificity is the number of CSS files; calculated by file count.
correctAnswer: Specificity is a weight based on selectors; calculated by counting IDs, classes, and elements.
explanation: Specificity is determined by a formula that assigns weights to ID selectors, class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, and type/pseudo-element selectors.

question: What are CSS custom properties (variables)?
options: They are global variables that can be used across all CSS files.
They are placeholders that get replaced during preprocessing.
They are properties prefixed with -- that can be defined and accessed at runtime.
They are functions that compute values based on other CSS properties.
correctAnswer: They are properties prefixed with -- that can be defined and accessed at runtime.
explanation: CSS custom properties are defined with a double hyphen prefix and are part of the live DOM, allowing runtime access via var().

question: How do CSS variables differ from preprocessor variables (like in SASS/LESS)?
options: CSS variables are static, preprocessor variables are dynamic.
CSS variables are evaluated at compile time, preprocessor variables at runtime.
CSS variables are part of the DOM and can change with JavaScript, preprocessor variables are resolved during compilation.
CSS variables cannot be used in media queries, preprocessor variables can.
correctAnswer: CSS variables are part of the DOM and can change with JavaScript, preprocessor variables are resolved during compilation.
explanation: CSS variables live in the rendered document and can be altered at runtime, whereas preprocessor variables are replaced during the build step.

question: What is the var() function and how do you provide a fallback value?
options: It declares a new variable; fallback is provided with a comma.
It retrieves a custom property value; fallback is the second argument after a comma.
It calculates a value; fallback is specified with an equals sign.
It sets a variable's default; fallback is defined with a semicolon.
correctAnswer: It retrieves a custom property value; fallback is the second argument after a comma.
explanation: var(--name, fallback) returns the custom property value or the fallback if the property is undefined.

question: What is the calc() function used for in CSS?
options: To perform arithmetic operations on values.
To calculate the size of the viewport.
To convert units between px and em.
To create responsive images.
correctAnswer: To perform arithmetic operations on values.
explanation: calc() allows addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of CSS values at runtime.

question: What is the difference between min(), max(), and clamp() functions in CSS?
options: min() returns the smallest value, max() returns the largest, clamp() limits a value between min and max.
min() and max() are for media queries, clamp() is for font sizes.
min() and max() are deprecated, clamp() is the new standard.
min() and max() only work with percentages, clamp() works with lengths.
correctAnswer: min() returns the smallest value, max() returns the largest, clamp() limits a value between min and max.
explanation: min() and max() return the minimum or maximum of their arguments, while clamp() constrains a value within a specified range.

question: How does inheritance work with CSS custom properties?
options: They are inherited by default like color.
They are not inherited unless explicitly set.
They are inherited only by elements that have the same selector.
They are inherited only if the property is defined on the root element.
correctAnswer: They are inherited by default like color.
explanation: Custom properties are inherited by default, just like other inheritable CSS properties.

question: What is the @property rule and how does it enhance CSS custom properties?
options: It defines custom property syntax for browsers.
It allows custom properties to be animated.
It registers custom properties for use in @property.
It sets default values for custom properties.
correctAnswer: It defines custom property syntax for browsers.
explanation: The @property rule declares the syntax of a custom property, enabling features such as animation and type checking.

question: What is a CSS media query and how is it used for responsive design?
options: A rule that applies styles based on media type.
A rule that applies styles based on viewport size.
A rule that applies styles based on device orientation.
All of the above.
correctAnswer: All of the above.
explanation: Media queries can target media type, viewport width, orientation, and other features to adapt styles.

question: What is the difference between mobile-first and desktop-first responsive design approaches?
options: Mobile-first starts with large screens, desktop-first starts with small screens.
Mobile-first starts with small screens, desktop-first starts with large screens.
Mobile-first uses only CSS, desktop-first uses CSS and JS.
No difference.
correctAnswer: Mobile-first starts with small screens, desktop-first starts with large screens.
explanation: Mobile-first defines base styles for small screens and adds media queries for larger ones, while desktop-first does the opposite.

question: What is the viewport meta tag's relationship with CSS media queries?
options: It sets the viewport width for media queries to reference.
It overrides media queries.
It is unrelated.
It only affects mobile browsers.
correctAnswer: It sets the viewport width for media queries to reference.
explanation: The viewport meta tag defines the layout viewport width, which media queries use to determine which styles to apply.

question: What is the CSS cascade and how does it determine which styles apply?
options: The cascade is the order of CSS files that are loaded.
The cascade is the process of resolving conflicts based on origin, importance, specificity, and source order.
The cascade is a way to cascade colors through a page.
The cascade is a CSS property that applies to all elements.
correctAnswer: The cascade is the process of resolving conflicts based on origin, importance, specificity, and source order.
explanation: The cascade resolves conflicts by considering the style origin, importance (!important), specificity of selectors, and the order in which rules appear.

question: What is CSS inheritance and which properties are inherited by default?
options: Inheritance is when child elements automatically get all styles from their parents.
Inheritance is when certain properties like color and font-family are passed to child elements by default.
Inheritance is a CSS function that copies styles to all descendants.
Inheritance only applies to block elements and not inline elements.
correctAnswer: Inheritance is when certain properties like color and font-family are passed to child elements by default.
explanation: Only a subset of properties, such as color, font-family, line-height, etc., are inherited automatically unless overridden.

question: What is the difference between the inherit, initial, and unset keywords?
options: inherit copies the parent value, initial sets the property to its default value, unset resets to inherited or initial depending on the property.
All three keywords perform the same action of resetting a property to its default value.
inherit sets the property to its default value, initial copies the parent value, unset does nothing.
None of the above.
correctAnswer: inherit copies the parent value, initial sets the property to its default value, unset resets to inherited or initial depending on the property.
explanation: inherit forces the property to adopt the parent’s value, initial forces the browser’s default, and unset reverts to the natural inheritance behavior.

question: What is the difference between source order and specificity in the cascade algorithm?
options: Specificity determines order, source order is ignored.
Source order is only used when specificity ties.
Specificity is only used for inline styles.
Source order is the same as specificity.
correctAnswer: Source order is only used when specificity ties.
explanation: When two rules have the same specificity, the one that appears later in the source wins.

question: What are CSS cascade layers (@layer) and what problem do they solve?
options: They group CSS rules into layers to control precedence, solving specificity wars.
They are used for layering background images only.
They are a new selector type for targeting nested elements.
They replace media queries for responsive design.
correctAnswer: They group CSS rules into layers to control precedence, solving specificity wars.
explanation: @layer lets developers define named layers that determine which rules win, making it easier to manage complex cascades and avoid specificity conflicts.

question: What is the difference between the all property and resetting individual properties?
options: all sets all properties at once; resetting individual properties only resets specified ones.
all only resets inherited properties; individual resets all.
all is shorthand for transition; individual resets only animations.
all is CSS variable; individual resets only custom properties.
correctAnswer: all sets all properties at once; resetting individual properties only resets specified ones.
explanation: The all property applies to every CSS property, resetting them to their initial or inherited values, whereas resetting individual properties only affects the properties you list.

question: Explain CSS animations and transitions. What is the difference?
options: Animations use @keyframes; transitions change property values over time.
Transitions use @keyframes; animations change property values over time.
Both are same; difference is vendor prefixes.
Animations are for layout changes; transitions are for color changes.
correctAnswer: Animations use @keyframes; transitions change property values over time.
explanation: Animations are defined with @keyframes and can run independently, while transitions automatically animate a change in a property when its value changes.

question: What is the transition-timing-function property and what values can it take?
options: It controls speed curve; values: linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier.
It sets duration; values: 1s, 2s, 3s.
It defines delay; values: 0s, 0.5s.
It sets property names; values: opacity, transform.
correctAnswer: It controls speed curve; values: linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier.
explanation: transition-timing-function determines how the intermediate values are calculated during a transition.

question: What are @keyframes in CSS and how are they used to define animations?
options: They define stages of animation; used with animation-name.
They set transition durations; used with transition property.
They declare CSS variables; used with :root.
They specify media queries; used with @media.
correctAnswer: They define stages of animation; used with animation-name.
explanation: An @keyframes rule lists the keyframes that describe the intermediate states of an animation.

question: What is the difference between animation-fill-mode values (none, forwards, backwards, both)?
options: none: no effect; forwards: retains final state; backwards: applies before start; both: applies both.
none: retains final state; forwards: no effect; backwards: applies after end; both: applies before start.
none: applies before start; forwards: after end; backwards: none; both: both.
none: applies after end; forwards: before start; backwards: both; both: none.
correctAnswer: none: no effect; forwards: retains final state; backwards: applies before start; both: applies both.
explanation: animation-fill-mode controls how the animation applies styles before it starts and after it ends.

question: What is the will-change CSS property and when should you use it?
options: It hints the browser to pre-render an element for future changes, used before heavy animations
It changes the color of an element
It changes the layout of an element
It changes the font of an element
correctAnswer: It hints the browser to pre-render an element for future changes, used before heavy animations
explanation: will-change tells the browser to optimize the element for upcoming changes, reducing repaint costs.

question: What is the difference between animating with CSS transforms/opacity vs animating layout properties like width/height, in terms of performance?
options: Transforms and opacity are composited and avoid layout reflow, making them faster
Width and height are composited and faster
Transforms cause reflow and are slower
Width and height cause compositing and are faster
correctAnswer: Transforms and opacity are composited and avoid layout reflow, making them faster
explanation: Changing transform or opacity only affects the compositor layer, while width/height triggers layout and paint.

question: What is the transform property and what are common 2D and 3D transform functions?
options: It moves an element in 2D/3D space; functions include translate, rotate, scale, skew, perspective
It changes the color of an element
It changes the font of an element
It changes the layout of an element
correctAnswer: It moves an element in 2D/3D space; functions include translate, rotate, scale, skew, perspective
explanation: The transform property applies geometric transformations; common functions are translate, rotate, scale, skew, and perspective.

question: What is hardware/GPU acceleration in CSS animations and how do you trigger it?
options: It offloads rendering to the GPU, triggered by using transform or opacity changes or setting translateZ(0)
It offloads rendering to the CPU, triggered by color changes
It offloads rendering to the GPU, triggered by width changes
It offloads rendering to the CPU, triggered by transform changes
correctAnswer: It offloads rendering to the GPU, triggered by using transform or opacity changes or setting translateZ(0)
explanation: GPU acceleration is achieved when the browser can render changes on a separate GPU layer, which happens with transforms, opacity, or translateZ(0).

question: What is the difference between animation-iteration-count: infinite and a fixed count?
options: Infinite repeats forever, fixed repeats a specified number of times
Infinite repeats once, fixed repeats forever
Infinite repeats a specified number of times, fixed repeats forever
Infinite repeats forever, fixed repeats once
correctAnswer: Infinite repeats forever, fixed repeats a specified number of times
explanation: The infinite value causes the animation to loop indefinitely; a numeric value limits the number of iterations.

question: What is FLIP technique in the context of CSS/JS animations?
options: A method to flip elements horizontally.
A technique for optimizing animations by capturing positions before and after changes.
A library for 3D transformations.
A CSS property for flipping content.
correctAnswer: A technique for optimizing animations by capturing positions before and after changes.
explanation: FLIP stands for First, Last, Invert, Play; it captures element positions before and after changes, calculates delta, and animates smoothly.

question: What is CSS-in-JS and what are its trade-offs?
options: Writing CSS inside JavaScript files, enabling scoped styles but increasing bundle size.
Using CSS files inside JavaScript functions, which reduces performance.
A technique to convert CSS to JavaScript objects, eliminating the need for CSS files.
A method to embed CSS directly in HTML tags.
correctAnswer: Writing CSS inside JavaScript files, enabling scoped styles but increasing bundle size.
explanation: CSS-in-JS writes styles as JS objects or template literals, providing scoped, dynamic styles at the cost of larger bundles and runtime overhead.

question: What is BEM (Block Element Modifier) naming convention and why is it used?
options: A naming convention that uses hyphens to separate words.
A methodology for naming CSS classes to avoid specificity issues and improve maintainability.
A tool for automatically generating CSS.
A CSS preprocessor.
correctAnswer: A methodology for naming CSS classes to avoid specificity issues and improve maintainability.
explanation: BEM structures class names into block__element--modifier, creating clear, reusable, low-specificity styles.

question: What is the difference between utility-first CSS (like Tailwind) and traditional semantic CSS?
options: Utility-first uses pre-built classes for common styles, while semantic uses descriptive class names for components.
Utility-first is only for JavaScript frameworks.
Semantic CSS is always faster to load.
Tailwind is a CSS preprocessor.
correctAnswer: Utility-first uses pre-built classes for common styles, while semantic uses descriptive class names for components.
explanation: Utility-first provides many small, single-purpose classes; semantic CSS uses meaningful class names that describe the component.

question: What is a CSS preprocessor (like SASS or LESS) and what advantages does it offer?
options: A tool that compiles CSS from a higher-level language, adding variables, nesting, mixins.
A browser extension for debugging CSS.
A CSS property that allows preprocessing of images.
A method to minify CSS.
correctAnswer: A tool that compiles CSS from a higher-level language, adding variables, nesting, mixins.
explanation: Preprocessors let you write more maintainable code with variables, nesting, mixins, then compile to plain CSS.

question: What is the difference between SASS's @mixin and @extend?
options: @mixin allows you to define reusable blocks of CSS that can accept arguments, while @extend merges selectors to share the same rules.
@mixin merges selectors, @extend defines reusable blocks with arguments.
Both do the same thing, just different syntax.
@mixin is only for variables, @extend is for mixins.
correctAnswer: @mixin allows you to define reusable blocks of CSS that can accept arguments, while @extend merges selectors to share the same rules.
explanation: @mixin creates reusable style blocks (optionally with parameters) that are included where needed; @extend merges selectors so they share the same rule set, reducing duplication.

question: What is PostCSS and how is it different from a preprocessor like SASS?
options: PostCSS is a JavaScript-based tool that uses plugins to transform CSS, operating on standard CSS, whereas SASS is a preprocessor that adds its own syntax and compiles to CSS.
PostCSS is a CSS preprocessor that adds variables and nesting.
PostCSS compiles SCSS to CSS.
PostCSS is a browser engine.
correctAnswer: PostCSS is a JavaScript-based tool that uses plugins to transform CSS, operating on standard CSS, whereas SASS is a preprocessor that adds its own syntax and compiles to CSS.
explanation: PostCSS works on plain CSS with a plugin ecosystem, while SASS introduces its own syntax (SCSS/Sass) that must be compiled to CSS.

question: What is CSS Modules and how do they solve the global namespace problem?
options: CSS Modules scope class names locally by generating unique identifiers, preventing clashes across components.
CSS Modules combine all CSS into a single global file.
CSS Modules use !important to override global styles.
CSS Modules are a type of preprocessor.
correctAnswer: CSS Modules scope class names locally by generating unique identifiers, preventing clashes across components.
explanation: Each class name is transformed into a unique hash, so styles are component‑scoped and do not pollute the global namespace.

question: What is critical CSS and why is it used for performance optimization?
options: Critical CSS is the minimal CSS required to render above-the-fold content, inlined to reduce render‑blocking resources.
Critical CSS is the CSS that is loaded after the page is fully rendered.
Critical CSS is a CSS framework for critical UI components.
Critical CSS refers to CSS that contains errors.
correctAnswer: Critical CSS is the minimal CSS required to render above-the-fold content, inlined to reduce render‑blocking resources.
explanation: Inlining only the styles needed for initial view eliminates render‑blocking network requests, speeding up first paint.

question: What is the ITCSS (Inverted Triangle CSS) methodology?
options: ITCSS is a layered architecture that organizes CSS from generic, low-specificity rules at the base to high-specificity, component‑specific rules at the top.
ITCSS is a CSS preprocessor.
ITCSS stands for Inline Tailwind CSS System.
ITCSS is a JavaScript library for styling.
correctAnswer: ITCSS is a layered architecture that organizes CSS from generic, low-specificity rules at the base to high-specificity, component‑specific rules at the top.
explanation: ITCSS structures styles in a logical hierarchy (settings, tools, generic, elements, objects, components, utilities) to manage specificity and scalability.

question: What is the difference between atomic CSS and component-scoped CSS?
options: Atomic CSS uses single-purpose classes, component-scoped CSS encapsulates styles within a component.
Atomic CSS is scoped to components, component-scoped CSS uses utility classes.
Both are the same.
Atomic CSS is only for layout, component-scoped CSS is for typography.
correctAnswer: Atomic CSS uses single-purpose classes, component-scoped CSS encapsulates styles within a component.
explanation: Atomic CSS focuses on reusable utility classes that apply one style at a time, while component-scoped CSS keeps styles tied to a specific component, preventing leakage.

question: What is reflow and repaint in CSS rendering, and how can you minimize them?
options: Reflow recalculates layout, repaint updates pixels; minimize by batching DOM changes and using transform/opacity.
Reflow updates pixels, repaint recalculates layout; minimize by using display:none.
Both are same; minimize by using CSS variables.
Reflow is only for animations; repaint is only for static pages.
correctAnswer: Reflow recalculates layout, repaint updates pixels; minimize by batching DOM changes and using transform/opacity.
explanation: Reflow (layout) recomputes geometry; repaint (painting) updates pixels. Grouping DOM changes and using transforms/opacity avoids layout thrashing.

question: What is the difference between properties that trigger layout, paint, and composite in the browser rendering pipeline?
options: Layout triggers reflow, paint triggers repaint, composite triggers compositing layers.
Paint triggers reflow, layout triggers repaint, composite triggers layout.
Composite triggers reflow, paint triggers layout, layout triggers composite.
None of the above.
correctAnswer: Layout triggers reflow, paint triggers repaint, composite triggers compositing layers.
explanation: Layout properties (e.g., width, height) cause reflow; paint properties (e.g., background-color) cause repaint; composite properties (e.g., transform, opacity) trigger compositing.

question: What is the content-visibility CSS property used for?
options: It allows the browser to skip rendering of offscreen content to improve performance.
It controls the visibility of text content only.
It is used to hide images.
It sets the opacity of an element.
correctAnswer: It allows the browser to skip rendering of offscreen content to improve performance.
explanation: content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip layout, paint, and compositing for hidden or offscreen content, boosting performance.

question: What is the difference between using transform: translate() and changing top/left for positioning animations, performance-wise?
options: transform: translate() uses GPU compositing and is smoother; top/left triggers layout and is slower.
top/left uses GPU compositing; transform: translate() triggers layout.
Both are identical in performance.
transform: translate() only works on block elements.
correctAnswer: transform: translate() uses GPU compositing and is smoother; top/left triggers layout and is slower.
explanation: transform creates a compositing layer and avoids layout changes, making animations smoother compared to top/left which forces reflow.

question: What is the purpose of the contain CSS property?
options: To specify the containment of an element's layout, painting, and style calculations.
To define the background color of an element.
To set the width and height of an element.
To control the visibility of an element.
correctAnswer: To specify the containment of an element's layout, painting, and style calculations.
explanation: The contain property limits the scope of layout, paint, and style calculations to improve performance.

question: How does the browser compute the CSSOM and combine it with the DOM to build the render tree?
options: It parses CSS into a CSSOM, then walks the DOM, matching selectors to build render tree nodes.
It merges CSSOM and DOM into a single tree before layout.
It ignores CSSOM and uses only DOM.
It builds render tree from CSSOM only.
correctAnswer: It parses CSS into a CSSOM, then walks the DOM, matching selectors to build render tree nodes.
explanation: The browser creates a CSSOM from stylesheets, then traverses the DOM to match rules and construct the render tree.

question: What is the difference between visibility: hidden and opacity: 0?
options: visibility: hidden removes the element from the layout flow, opacity: 0 keeps it in flow but invisible.
visibility: hidden keeps the element in flow but invisible, opacity: 0 removes it from flow.
Both hide the element, but visibility: hidden makes it non-interactive while opacity: 0 keeps it interactive.
Both hide the element and make it non-interactive.
correctAnswer: Both hide the element, but visibility: hidden makes it non-interactive while opacity: 0 keeps it interactive.
explanation: visibility: hidden hides the element and disables interaction; opacity: 0 makes it fully transparent but still interactive and occupies space.

question: What is the difference between overflow: hidden, scroll, and auto?
options: hidden hides overflow content, scroll always shows scrollbars, auto shows scrollbars only when needed.
hidden shows scrollbars only when needed, scroll hides overflow, auto always shows scrollbars.
hidden shows scrollbars always, scroll hides overflow, auto shows scrollbars only when needed.
hidden hides overflow content, scroll shows scrollbars only when needed, auto always shows scrollbars.
correctAnswer: hidden hides overflow content, scroll always shows scrollbars, auto shows scrollbars only when needed.
explanation: overflow: hidden clips content, scroll forces scrollbars, auto shows them only if content overflows.

question: What is the CSS box-shadow property and how do its parameters work?
options: It adds a shadow to an element; parameters are offset-x, offset-y, blur-radius, spread-radius, and color.
It adds a border; parameters are width, style, color.
It changes background; parameters are color and opacity.
It adds a gradient; parameters are direction and color stops.
correctAnswer: It adds a shadow to an element; parameters are offset-x, offset-y, blur-radius, spread-radius, and color.
explanation: box-shadow creates a shadow with specified offsets, blur, spread, and color to enhance visual depth.

question: What is the difference between linear-gradient and radial-gradient in CSS?
options: linear-gradient draws a gradient along a straight line, while radial-gradient draws a gradient radiating from a center point.
linear-gradient uses color stops, while radial-gradient uses only two colors.
linear-gradient only works on backgrounds, while radial-gradient works on borders.
linear-gradient is CSS3, while radial-gradient is CSS4.
correctAnswer: linear-gradient draws a gradient along a straight line, while radial-gradient draws a gradient radiating from a center point.
explanation: linear-gradient creates a gradient along a straight axis, whereas radial-gradient creates a circular or elliptical gradient that radiates from a center point.

question: What is the object-fit property used for on images and videos?
options: to control how the element's content is resized to fit its container.
to set the opacity of the element.
to define the aspect ratio of the element.
to apply a filter effect.
correctAnswer: to control how the element's content is resized to fit its container.
explanation: object-fit specifies how the content of a replaced element (image/video) should be resized to fit its box, e.g., contain, cover, fill, etc.

question: What is the difference between currentColor and inherit for color values?
options: currentColor uses the element's computed color; inherit passes the color from the parent.
currentColor inherits from parent; inherit uses the element's own color.
currentColor is a keyword for black; inherit is for transparent.
currentColor is only for text; inherit is for background.
correctAnswer: currentColor uses the element's computed color; inherit passes the color from the parent.
explanation: currentColor refers to the element's own color value, while inherit forces the property to take the value from its parent element.

question: What is the writing-mode property used for in CSS?
options: to set the direction in which text is laid out (horizontal or vertical).
to rotate the entire page.
to change the font size.
to control line spacing.
correctAnswer: to set the direction in which text is laid out (horizontal or vertical).
explanation: writing-mode controls the flow of text, allowing horizontal, vertical, or sideways writing.

question: What is the difference between the ch, vw, vh, and vmin/vmax units?
options: ch is based on the width of the '0' character; vw/vh are viewport width/height; vmin/vmax are the smaller/larger of vw and vh.
ch is viewport width; vw/vh are character width; vmin/vmax are viewport height.
ch is for color; vw/vh for width; vmin/vmax for maximum.
ch is for font size; vw/vh for vertical height; vmin/vmax for minimum.
correctAnswer: ch is based on the width of the '0' character; vw/vh are viewport width/height; vmin/vmax are the smaller/larger of vw and vh.
explanation: ch measures relative to the '0' glyph width, vw/vh are percentages of the viewport, and vmin/vmax are the min/max of vw and vh respectively.
